newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa running out of time for labour bill.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa running out of time for labour bill.

text.p: Barely a week before the deadline for adoption of a new employment law, the government's negotiating partners remained deadlocked on key clauses, Labour Minister Tito Mboweni said in an interview.

Mboweni said the government was talking separately to labour and business delegates to the National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) in a bid to ensure passage of the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill through parliament this year.
"We are not having any trilateral negotiations at the moment. The parties don't want to meet in any trilateral setting, so we are having bilateral negotiations," he told Reuters.
"Our discussions have resulted in some significant progress on a whole range of areas, but have created deadlocks on a few.
"If by the 15th of August we have not been able to make any progress at all, no movement, nothing, then we are in serious difficulties," he said.
Mboweni said it was essential to achieve broad consensus by Friday next week, but added that some specific details could be resolved over the next two weeks.
Mboweni said key proposals which remained in dispute were:
- The bill's proposal for four months of maternity leave, which business considers excessive and labour wants extended to six months.

- The proposed reduction of the maximum working week from between 46 and 60 hours to 45 hours for all. Labour wants a commitment in the bill to a 40-hour week within a specific period. Business opposes even a non-binding statement of intent.
- The proposed minimum employment age of 15 -- the minimum school-leaving age -- which labour wants raised to 16.

- The proposed increase in overtime rates from a minimum of time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half, with business seeking an averaging provision to account for production peaks and labour opposed to a longer measure than a single week.
- The latitude for agreement in formal bargaining forums to exemption from some aspects of the bill, which business wants extended and labour wants reduced.
Mboweni said he would not assume sole responsibility for the bill if government's labour and business partners failed to agree on a formulation.

"I am insisting that the parties must agree.... We must take these difficult decisions together. If we don't agree by next Friday, there is a very real danger that the bill may just wither away," he said.
Mboweni said parties appeared to be on track to agree terms for the payment of maternity leave benefits out of the state-run Unemployment Insurance Fund.
He said he expected a compromise on Sunday work according to which regular Sunday workers would be paid time-and-a-half while occasional Sunday workers would get double time.

"On overtime rates, I think we are going to stand by what's in the bill, which is that we move from time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half. We are going to stand by that and business is going to have to reorganise itself in that regard," he said.
